module

public import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Erdős Problem 1007

*References:*
- [erdosproblems.com/1007](https://www.erdosproblems.com/1007)
- [ChNo16] Chaffee, Joe and Noble, Matt, *Dimension 4 and dimension 5 graphs with minimum edge
  set*. Australas. J. Combin. (2016), 327-333.
- [Ho13] House, Roger F., *A 4-dimensional graph has at least 9 edges*. Discrete Math. (2013),
  1783-1789.
-/

@[expose] public section

namespace Erdos1007

open scoped EuclideanGeometry

variable {V : Type*}

/-- The complete tripartite graph $K_{1,3,3}$. -/
abbrev K133 := SimpleGraph.completeMultipartiteGraph fun i : Fin 3 => Fin (![1, 3, 3] i)

/--
The dimension of a graph $G$ is the minimal $n$ such that $G$ can be embedded in $\mathbb{R}^n$
such that every edge of $G$ is a unit line segment.

What is the smallest number of edges in a graph with dimension $4$?

Answer: The smallest number of edges is $9$, achieved solely by $K_{3,3}$, proved by House [Ho13]. An
alternative proof was given by Chaffee and Noble [ChNo16], who also prove that the smallest
number of edges in a graph of dimension $5$ is $15$ (achieved by $K_6$ and $K_{1,3,3}$).
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 5 52, formal_proof using lean4 at "https://github.com/plby/lean-proofs/blob/main/src/v4.29.1/ErdosProblems/Erdos1007.lean"]
theorem erdos_1007 :
    IsLeast {m | ∃ (n : ℕ) (G : SimpleGraph (Fin n)), G.HasDimension 4 ∧ G.edgeSet.ncard = m}
      9 := by
  sorry

/--
The smallest number of edges in a graph of dimension $4$ is achieved solely by $K_{3,3}$.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 5 52]
theorem erdos_1007.variants.dimension_four_extremal (n : ℕ) (G : SimpleGraph (Fin n))
    (hdim : G.HasDimension 4) (hcard : G.edgeSet.ncard = 9)
    (hdeg : ∀ v : Fin n, ∃ w : Fin n, G.Adj v w) :
    Nonempty (G ≃g completeBipartiteGraph (Fin 3) (Fin 3)) := by
  sorry

/--
The smallest number of edges in a graph of dimension $5$ is $15$.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 5 52]
theorem erdos_1007.variants.dimension_five :
    IsLeast {m | ∃ (n : ℕ) (G : SimpleGraph (Fin n)), G.HasDimension 5 ∧ G.edgeSet.ncard = m}
      15 := by
  sorry

/--
The smallest number of edges in a graph of dimension $5$ is achieved by $K_6$ and $K_{1,3,3}$.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 5 52]
theorem erdos_1007.variants.dimension_five_extremal :
    ((SimpleGraph.completeGraph (Fin 6)).HasDimension 5 ∧
        (SimpleGraph.completeGraph (Fin 6)).edgeSet.ncard = 15) ∧
      (K133.HasDimension 5 ∧ K133.edgeSet.ncard = 15) := by
  sorry

end Erdos1007

reformulations.difference: The source's terse uniqueness statement (Chaffee–Noble, Theorem 7) says that the only dimension-four graph with nine edges is K₃,₃. Lean explicitly excludes isolated vertices through hdeg and states uniqueness up to graph isomorphism.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: The source's uniqueness claim necessarily disregards isolated vertices. For a finite graph with edges, deleting isolated vertices preserves both edge count and dimension: embeddings restrict to the remaining vertices, and embeddings in any positive dimension extend by placing the finitely many isolated vertices at distinct unused points. Consequently, uniqueness after deleting isolated vertices is equivalent to uniqueness among graphs satisfying hdeg. The additional hypothesis makes this necessary convention explicit rather than excluding a genuine extremal configuration.

review.notes: Checked K133 and all four theorem statements against the cited Chaffee–Noble paper. The dimension definition correctly requires injectivity without requiring an induced representation. Fin n covers finite graphs up to relabelling, and every edge set used here is finite. The scratch file /workspace/review/scratch.lean compiles: it verifies the three edge counts, expands both minimum statements into attainment plus a universal lower bound, identifies hdeg with full vertex support, and checks empty/singleton and edgeless boundary cases. The Erdős webpage and House's full text were inaccessible; Chaffee–Noble explicitly states and proves all relevant results, including House's uniqueness result. The external proof's conclusion is equivalent and its file contains no explicit sorry or custom axioms. Its original Lean/Mathlib 4.29.1 proof was not independently kernel-verified: compilation under the available 4.33.1 encountered version/API incompatibilities, which are not evidence of a mathematical or status defect.
